paras: The killing of Levi Lally was the fatal shooting of a farmer at his house near Montevallo, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, July 21, 1888, by two white men and a Black man who had called him outside. Lally died the next day, and warrants were issued on suspicion against men with whom he had quarrelled over work. The case reached distant papers through a single Montgomery dispatch, and a moonshiner killing in Bibb County, reported about ten days later, bore some resemblance to it.

According to the Montgomery dispatch, someone came to Lally's house on Saturday night "pretending to ask the way to Brierfield." When Lally came out he found two white men and "a negro," who at once opened fire on him. Nine shots were fired at him, and he died of his wounds the following day. The reports do not state Lally's race or name any of the attackers.

Warrants were issued "on suspicion" against "some persons with whom he had a disagreement about work," and the dispatch added that "the country round about is much excited." No report of an arrest, inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News printed the dispatch on its front page under "Called Out and Shot," with the subhead "Two White Men and a Negro Parties to an Assassination." The Richmond Dispatch ran the same text the same day under "Murdered at Night," spelling the town "Montevale." Both papers treated it as a brief telegraphic item, foregrounding the attackers' mixed races in the Savannah headline but offering no comment on motive beyond the work dispute.

Coverage of a moonshiner gang in Bibb County, which began about ten days later, was far wider and more lurid. Under headlines such as "Human Hyenas in a Hole" and "Murderous Moonshiners," papers from Savannah to Indianapolis, Richmond and Austin reported that a citizens' posse had trapped the gang in a drift of the Brierfield coal mines and planned to starve them out. None of those reports mentioned Lally by name.

A Montgomery item of August 1 said the besieged gang was "the same one that called Mr. Lawley from his house about a week ago and killed him," adding that Lawley had informed revenue officers. Later Birmingham dispatches named the victim "Jack Lawly" or "Jack Lowley," a prominent Bibb County citizen who had guided United States officers, and accused moonshiners named Snyder, Bill Ray, Jim Hickey and an unnamed Black man of calling him out and shooting him. The method, the presence of a Black man among the attackers and the Brierfield setting resemble the Lally killing, but the name, county and stated motive differ. The Birmingham reports also placed the Lawley killing on "Last Sunday," a week after Lally was shot, and one said the victim was murdered "for his money," so the coverage does not establish that the two were the same man.

bases: The only reports naming Lally describe a night-time shooting by three men (two white, one Black) after a dispute over work, with no mob, band or crowd reported (A1, A2).
Both reports naming Lally carry the same Montgomery wire dispatch (A1, A2); the later moonshiner reports of a 'Lawley' killing are not tied to Lally by name (A3, A8, A9).

accounts.label: Montgomery wire (Lally)
accounts.gist: Lally was lured out of his house at night by a false request for directions and shot nine times by two white men and a Black man; warrants were issued against men he had quarrelled with over work.

accounts.label: Montgomery and Birmingham wires (Lawley)
accounts.gist: A Bibb County moonshiner gang, including a Black man, called a prominent citizen named Lawley from his house and killed him, said variously to be for informing revenue officers or for his money; a citizens' posse besieged the gang in a Brierfield coal drift.

framing.detail: The Lally dispatch ran as a short wire item, headlined 'Called Out and Shot' with the subhead 'Two White Men and a Negro Parties to an Assassination' in Savannah and 'Murdered at Night' in Richmond.
The moonshiner coverage called the gang 'Human Hyenas', 'Murderous Moonshiners' and 'Desperadoes' and reported the posse's plan to starve them out without criticism.

versions.value: Levi Lally shot Saturday night and died the next day; warrants against men he had a disagreement with about work
Lawley called from his house 'about a week ago' by a moonshiner gang because he had given information to revenue officers
A prominent citizen waylaid and murdered 'for his money' 'Last Sunday night' by moonshiners
Lawly/Lowley, who had guided U.S. officers, called out of his house (or to his gate) 'Last Sunday' and shot dead (and robbed) by Snyder, Ray, Hickey and a Black man

conflicts.note: No report links the names Lally and Lawley. The shared details (called from the house at night, a Black man among white attackers, Brierfield nearby) suggest a possible garbled identity, but the motive, county and Sunday dates differ; the Birmingham dispatches dated July 31 and Aug. 2 put the Lawley killing on Sunday, July 29, a week after Lally was shot.
